title: The wrong comparison operator
summary: How using `=` instead of a comparison can change a boolean and make an `if` branch run unexpectedly.
objectives: Explain the difference between `=` and `==` in a condition.
Trace how assigning a boolean affects the condition and the variable.
Fix a condition that accidentally assigns a value.
Recognize the same mistake when assigning `true` or `false`.

blocks.text: A condition should ask a question, such as whether `ready` is `true`. A common mistake is to write `=` instead of `==`. In Java, `=` assigns a value. In a condition like `if (ready = true)`, it changes `ready` to `true`, then the condition is true. The program compiles, but it does not behave as intended.

bad.title: Assigns true instead of checking ready

good.title: Checks ready without changing it
good.output:
Door stays closed
ready is false

blocks.note: The bad program compiles. The assignment `ready = true` is itself a boolean expression, and its value is `true`. So the first branch runs, and `ready` changes. The good program checks the value of `ready` and leaves it unchanged.

blocks.text: The symbols look similar, but they do different jobs. Use `=` to put a value into a variable. Use `==` to ask whether two values are equal. In Java, an `if` condition must be a boolean: either `true` or `false`. Assigning `true` to a boolean variable produces a boolean value, so this mistake is allowed by the compiler.

blocks.caption: What happens when the condition uses assignment

blocks.title: Compile time and run time
blocks.text: This mistake is not rejected at compile time. The code compiles, usually without a warning, then changes the variable when it runs. The wrong branch is a run-time behavior problem, not a compile error.
A trace means following each action in order. Start with `ready` set to `false`. Then follow what the condition `ready = true` does.

blocks.caption: Tracing if (ready = true) when ready starts false

blocks.text: The change happens before Java chooses a branch. With the fixed condition `if (ready)`, Java checks the value without assigning a new one. Since `ready` is `false`, the `else` branch runs.

In the first example, the program should open the door only when `ready` is already `true`. Ask what the condition should do: change the value, or check the value? It should check, so use `if (ready)`.

bad.title: Unexpectedly opens the door

good.title: Opens only when ready is true

blocks.note: The starting value is `false`. The bad condition overwrites it with `true`, so it prints `Open`. The fixed condition reads the existing value, so it prints `Wait`.

blocks.text: In the second example, a student with a ticket should be allowed in. The bad condition assigns `false` to `hasTicket`, so the condition is false and the ticket value is lost. Check the existing value with `if (hasTicket)` instead.

bad.title: Assigns false and denies entry

good.title: Checks the ticket value

blocks.note: The bad assignment evaluates to `false`, so the `else` branch runs. The fixed condition checks the value and keeps `hasTicket` as `true`.

blocks.text: The mistake can assign either boolean value. In both cases, the condition changes the variable before the branch is chosen. A quick way to check your code is to ask whether the condition is meant to test a value or set one.

blocks.note: The bad version changes `hasPaid` to `true`. The good version checks its current value. For a boolean, `if (hasPaid)` is clearer than `if (hasPaid == true)`.
The `!` operator means not. The good version checks for a false value without changing `hasPaid`. The bad version sets it to `false`.

blocks.question: What does this condition do when `open` starts as `false`?
blocks.explanation: The assignment stores `true` in `open` and evaluates to `true`. The condition succeeds, so the branch prints `Open`. The code compiles because the condition is boolean.

blocks.question: A program should print `Welcome` only when `member` is already true. Which condition should it use?
blocks.explanation: The program should check the current value, not assign a new one. `if (member)` checks whether `member` is true.

blocks.question: What is the difference between these two operators?
blocks.explanation: In Java, `=` assigns a value to a variable. `==` compares two values and produces a boolean result.

items: `=` assigns a value. `==` compares two values for equality.
An assignment to a boolean can be used as an `if` condition because it evaluates to a boolean value.
`if (ready = true)` changes `ready` before choosing a branch, and it compiles.
For a boolean variable, write `if (ready)` to check for true and `if (!ready)` to check for false.
Trace the condition in order: check whether it changes a variable before deciding which branch runs.
